# Introduction

My initial foray into the realm of calculating multignerational kinship probabilities
ended with some nice recurrence relations for calculating sums of probabilities along
different branches of pedigrees.  However, this was a coarse-grained marginal calculation
and did not lend itself to properly calculating the first-hitting probabilities needed.
That effort had started with an elaborate notation scheme for denoting ancestral paths.
That notation, unfortunately, does not extend well to the multiple lineages that must be
treated in a pedigree.  Therefore, we are going back to tried and true visual representation
(not simply notation!) to help us think through the calculations and make them efficient.

The main visual apparatus I have been playing with is a combination: a pedigree 
combined with visual respresentations of the ancestral cohorts reachable from the cohorts
of the two samples, $A$ and $B$.  In putting this together it became clear that we really need
to keep track of all the branches of the pedigree going up, because the order in which
the sexes of the ancestors arrive makes a difference.  The easiest way to see that
is to have males and females with different reproductive schedules.  To that end,
for an example life history I have one in which males mature at age 3 and have a max
age of 10, while females mature at 6 and have a max age of 12.  The plotting functions
are implemented in my package `CKMRexplain' for the moment. Let's begin:
```{r}
library(CKMRexplain)
```

# A Handy Visual Representation

Any time we are tracing lineages back through a pedigree, we have a pedigree.  In
fact, for CKMR and calculating pairwise kinship probabilities, we always have
two pedigrees---one for each member of the pair.  We refer to these pair members
as $A$ and $B$.  Here is a representation of those two pedigrees.
```{r}
draw_pedigree_and_cohorts(showCohorts = FALSE, sexA = "M")
```

That shows two simple pedigrees that go back $n=3$ generations: one pedigree for $A$
on the left and one for $B$ on the right. Males are represented by squares and
females are represented by circles. The ancestors are
named by numbers (following the CKMRpop paper) and we assume that neither $A$ nor
$B$ is inbred.  To the left
of the figure is a reference bar that shows cohorts (birth-years). Note that more
recent cohorts are toward the bottom and cohorts from earlier in time are toward
the top.  $A$ and $B$ are positioned vertically at their birth years (56 and 60,
respectively), but above that the ancestors are simply distributed vertically so
that the top row is at the same place, and generations above either $A$ or $B$ are
spread evenly in the intervening space.  Each ancestor occupies a specific place
in the $x$-direction denoted by a dashed line.  This x-position is where we will
place additional ``cohort bars'' to indicate the possible cohorts that these
ancestors could have belonged to, given the cohorts of $A$ and $B$ and age range
over which males and females can reproduce.  

The following plot includes those cohort bars.  The bars for the female ancestors
are denoted in reddish colors and for the male ancestors in blue-ish colors.  As
we proceed back in time further in the pedigree the colors get lighter as an aid
to see which cohort bars represent parents, grandparents and great-grandparents
when scanning from left to right. 
```{r}
draw_pedigree_and_cohorts(
  showCohorts = TRUE,
  sexA = "M"
)
```

This is an incredibly helpful representation.  Staring at it for a moment, one
realizes that $A$ and $B$ have the possibility to share an ancestor every time
any male ancestor of $A$ is from the same cohort as any male ancestor from $B$,
and also when any female ancestor from $A$ is from the same cohort as any female
ancestor from $B$.  For example, if $A$'s father was from cohort 50, then simply
following the gray line at 50 across to $B$'s ancestors, we see that there is
the possibility that $A$'s father was the same as ancestor 2, 4, 8, or 6 of $B$.
(Whoa! This looks like things could explode combinatorically...we will have to
organize our calculations carefully, if possible).



And while we are at it, we can also note that $A$ would have
the possibility of being a direct ancestor of $B$ whenever $B$ has an ancestor
from the same cohort as the cohort of $A$.  

So, this representation tells us where the chances are for the two samples
to have a common ancestor: any time a male of $A$ is of the same cohort as a male
ancestor of $B$ or any time a female ancestor of $A$ is from the same cohort as
a female ancestor of $B$.  However, that is not the only part of the equation, because the
samples (and their subsequent ancestors) may come from different cohorts themselves,
and this means that we have to deal with the ancestor surviving during the years
intervening the cohorts of its descendants.

We are going to borrow some notation from my previous effort, but we will expand it.
Let $\HH{a}{b}(c_A, c_B)$ denote the event that $A$ and $B$ from cohorts $c_A$
and $c_B$ respectively share a single most-recent common ancestor that is $a$ generations
back in the past from $A$ and $b$ generations back from $B$. It is possible for $a$ or
$b$ to be zero, which implies a direct descent relationship.

First, we consider the sex-specific $\HH{1}{1}$ event that we will denote $\HH{1}{1}(c_A, c_B;s)$,
where $s$ denotes the sex of the shared ancestor.  It can be either 0 for female or 1 for male,
or where convenient we might use $\f$ and $\m$.  This
is the half-sibling kinship probability, and it will come up again and again.
To make it simpler we will just focus on $A$ an $B$ and one generation of ancestors
for this first round. The diagram looks like this:
```{r}
shared_H11 <- tibble::tibble(
  focalA = "A", focalB = "B",
  cohortA = 56, cohortB = 60,
  ancestorA = "A-2", ancestorB = "B-2"
)

draw_pedigree_and_cohorts(
  shared_H11 = shared_H11
)
```

One of the interesting things about this is that (barring weird spatial structure
which we are ignoring for the moment (but which we might be able to deal with) and
other weird effects) is that this has to apply to any pair of individuals from
similar cohorts (and similar covariates, I suppose.  That's where things get weird
but we can sort of integrate over all that).

As a consequence, we can think about any ancestor pair also having an $\HH{1}{1}$
relationship.  For example, what about A-3 and B-4, if they were assumed to have
been born in cohorts 44 and 42, respectively, could share female ancestors, one
generation back from each of A-7 and B-9.  That looks like:
```{r}
shared_H11_2 <- tibble::tibble(
  focalA = "A-3", focalB = "B-4",
  cohortA = 44, cohortB = 42,
  ancestorA = "A-7", ancestorB = "B-9"
)

draw_pedigree_and_cohorts(
  shared_H11 = shared_H11_2,
  focal_indiv_A = "A-3",  # color those cells fuschia, too
  focal_cohort_A = 44,
  focal_indiv_B = "B-4",
  focal_cohort_B = 42
)
```



This is super promising.  The main thing to see here is that the probability of being
a maternal half sibling given that the pair members are ancestors born in cohorts $c_1$ and $c_2$
does not depend on how you got to those ancestors in your lines of descent (again, barring
spatial stuff---or perhaps some other weird covariates that are inherited across generations).
What this means is that the half-sibling calculation is going to be the same for
every pair of cohorts $(c_1, c_2)$ regardless of which ancestor that is in.  This is
actually super powerful.  It means that we can calculate those $P(\HH{1}{1}(c_1,c_2;s))$
probs for all possible $(c_1, c_2)$ pairs, and then we can use the for every intermediate
ancestor.  

Now, when we are tracking lineages going back up through the pedigree, we need to consider the
joint and conditional probabilities that a pair shares a parent of sex $s$, or not, and that
the parents' cohorts are explicitly $c^*_A$ and $c^*_B$.  (Note, $A$ and $B$ don't really
have to be samples here---we can just use $A$ and $B$ to denote two individuals from the
population.)

So, let
$$
P\bigl(\HH{1}{1}(c_A,c_B;s) = 1\bigl)
$$
be the probability that $A$ ane $B$ share a sex-$s$ parent.  This is actually the
sum over all possible shared parent cohorts $c^*_A = c^*_B$ of the joint probability
that the that parents are of the same cohort $c^*$ and that they are one and the
same (i.e., the shared parents).  


I think I will try for some new notation for this.
Let $I(A^1_s)$ be the identity of the sex-$s$ parent of A, one generation back.  We
could extend this to be like $I(A^2_{s_2s_1})$ which is the identity of the ancestor
two generations back that is of sex $s_2$, whose intervening descendant is of sex
$s_1$.  So, for example, we could write $I(A^2_{\m\f})$ for A's maternal grandfather.
Also, let $C(A^1_s)$ be the cohort of the sex-$s$ ancestor one generation back from $A$.
So, we can express the half-sib probability with shared parent of sex $s$ as:
$$
P\biggl( I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\biggr)
$$
which can be written as a sum over the joint probability of the cohorts and shared identities
of the parents of $A$ and $B$:
$$
P\biggl( I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\biggr) = \sum_{c \in \{C(A^1_s)\} \cap \{C(B^1_s)\}} P\biggl(C(A^1_s) = c,~C(B^1_s) = c,~I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\biggr)
$$
where the sum in $c$ is over the intersection of feasible cohorts for the the sex-$s$
parents of $A$ and $B$.  It is worth pointing out here that the joint probability
can be written as the probability that the two sex-$s$ parents are from the same
cohort times the probability that they are the same individual given they are from the
same cohort:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P\biggl(C(A^1_s) = c,~C(B^1_s) = c,~I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\biggr) &= 
     P\biggl(C(A^1_s) = c\biggr) 
     P\biggl(C(B^1_s) = c\biggr) \\
& \times P\biggl(I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)~\biggl|~ C(A^1_s) = c,~C(B^1_s) = c \biggr).
\end{aligned}
$$
And that is simply lovely because we already know that $P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c\bigr)$ and
$P\biggl(C(B^1_s) = c\biggr)$ are simply the expected relative reproductive output of 
sex-$s$ individuals from cohort $c$ at the time of $A$ or $B$'s birth respectively.
And $P\bigl(I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)~\bigl|~ C(A^1_s) = c,~C(B^1_s) = c \bigr)$ is just
where we have 1 over the number of cohort-c individuals of sex $s$ at the time of
the second-born's birth, and the survival term in there.  So that is all very familiar.
But that is typically as far as it goes---you just calculate the HSP prob and you are done.
But, when we are trying to think through a general calculation for multigenerational
kinship probabilities, there are a few more terms that will be very important.

One term that isn't really used for the multigenerational bit is the conditional
probability that the cohort of the shared parent is $c$ given that pair does 
share a sex-$s$ parent.  This follows simply from the law of conditional
probability:
$$
P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c,~C(B^1_s) = c \mid I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\bigr) =
\frac{P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c,~C(B^1_s) = c,~I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\bigr)}
{P\bigl( I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\bigr)}
$$
I say that this term is not much used for the multigenerational kinship because
if we find that a pair is an HSP, then we don't go any further back in the pedigree
to see if they are more distantly related.  However, it is worth writing that down
because it gets us primed up to understand the much more important conditional
probability for our purposes, which is the conditional probability that the sex-$s$ parent of
$A$ was from cohort $c_A$, and the sex-$s$ parent of $B$ was from cohort $c_B$ given
that $A$ and $B$ do _not_ share a sex-$s$ parent.  This is actually the probability that
we need for weighting ancestral cohorts when we  continue extending the lineages back into past 
generations, so it is pretty important.  We write this as:
$$
P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c_A,~C(B^1_s) = c_B \mid I(A^1_s) \neq I(B^1_s)\bigr) =
\frac{P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c_A,~C(B^1_s) = c_B,~I(A^1_s) \neq  I(B^1_s)\bigr)}
{1 - P\bigl( I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\bigr)}
$$
(Note that $P\bigl( I(A^1_s) \neq  I(B^1_s)\bigr) = 1 - P\bigl( I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\bigr)$, so
we write it that way in the denominator.  Also, note that if $c_A\neq c_B$ then
$I(A^1_s) \neq I(B^1_s)$ with probability 1.  So we have that this is essentially
$$
=\begin{cases}
\frac{P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c_A,~C(B^1_s) = c_B\bigr)}
{1 - P\bigl( I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\bigr)}~~~~&\mbox{when}~~c_A \neq c_B  \\
\frac{P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c,~C(B^1_s) = c,~I(A^1_s) \neq I(B^1_s)\bigr)}
{1 - P\bigl( I(A^1_s) =  I(B^1_s)\bigr)}~~~~&\mbox{when}~~c_A = c_B = c
\end{cases}
$$
The $P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c_A,~C(B^1_s) = c_B\bigr)$ term is just the product of
the ERROs for those cohorts of parents.  So, we know how to get those.  When
$c_A = c_B = c$ and the identities of the parents are not the same, that can occur
because either the parent of the first born did not survive (so we would have
a $1 - \prod \lambda$ term in there), OR because it did survive, but was not the
parent of the second born (in which case it has a $\prod \lambda$ multiplied by
a $\frac{N-1}{N}$ term).  We can verify these to make sure that the unnormalized conditional
probabilities (i.e., the joint probabilities) sum to 1 over all $c_A$ and $c_B$ and
over $I(A^1_s) = I(B^1_s)$ and $I(A^1_s) \neq I(B^1_s)$


I like this notation and where it is going.  But sometime around now is when we
need to start considering our first "large population approximation" by which
we assert that only a single lineage will coalesce at any particular
generational level (unless it is an F-type relationship, and we have a different
way of dealing with that (only in same cohorts!)). I think that this is
going to be a crucial assumption/assertion to avoid combinatorically blowing up
when we get lots of overlapping lineages.  It is also a reasonable one, and one
that is analagous to the common assumption in CKMR that we end up only with pairs.
One of the first places we can apply this assumption is when we are considering the
lineages coming up through both the male and the female parents.  As we have seen
above, it is straightforward to calculate both
$$
P\bigl(C(A^1_\m) = c,~C(B^1_\m) = c \mid I(A^1_\m) =  I(B^1_\m)\bigr)
$$
and 
$$
P\bigl(C(A^1_\f) = c,~C(B^1_\f) = c \mid I(A^1_\f) =  I(B^1_\f)\bigr).
$$
Those are both marginal probabilities for the male and female parents; however, if
we want to entertain the idea of tracing lineages further back in time given that
neither the male nor the female parent was shared between $A$ and $B$, then we
will need to calculate the conditional probability of the cohorts of the parents of
$A$ and $B$ given that none of the parents were shared.  This will look something
like:
\begin{equation}
  (\#eq:parent-cohorts-unshared)
\frac{P\bigl(C(A^1_\m) = c^\m_A,~C(B^1_\m) = c^\m_B,~
       C(A^1_\f) = c^\f_A,~C(B^1_\f) = c^\f_B,~ 
       I(A^1_\m) \neq  I(B^1_\m),~I(A^1_\f) \neq  I(B^1_\f)
       \bigr)
}{
P\bigl( 
       I(A^1_\m) \neq  I(B^1_\m),~I(A^1_\f) \neq  I(B^1_\f)
       \bigr)
}
\end{equation}
Let's say we assume that mating is totally at random so that mothers and fathers
are independent.  In that case, the numerator is no problem: it factorizes into
\begin{equation}
(\#eq:pcu-numer)
P\bigl(C(A^1_\m) = c^\m_A,~C(B^1_\m) = c^\m_B \mid
       I(A^1_\m) \neq  I(B^1_\m)
       \bigr) \times
P\bigl( C(A^1_\f) = c^\f_A,~C(B^1_\f) = c^\f_B \mid I(A^1_\f) \neq  I(B^1_\f) \bigr).
\end{equation}
The harder nut to crack is the denominator because of inclusion/exclusion.  We note that
\begin{equation}
(\#eq:pcu-denom)
\begin{aligned}
P\bigl( 
       I(A^1_\m) \neq  I(B^1_\m),~I(A^1_\f) \neq  I(B^1_\f)
       \bigr) &= 1 - 
P\bigl( 
       I(A^1_\m) =  I(B^1_\m) \bigr)  \\
&- P\bigl( 
       I(A^1_\f) =  I(B^1_\f) \bigr) \\
&+ P\bigl( 
       I(A^1_\m) =  I(B^1_\m),~I(A^1_\f) =  I(B^1_\f)
       \bigr),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
and remind ourselves that $P\bigl(I(A^1_\m) =  I(B^1_\m) \bigr)$ and
$P\bigl(I(A^1_\f) =  I(B^1_\f) \bigr)$ are easy to compute by summing
over the possible shared cohorts.  The term
$P\bigl(I(A^1_\m) =  I(B^1_\m),~I(A^1_\f) =  I(B^1_\f)\bigr)$, however, might
be a little more involved to compute.  Or is it?  If the shared nature of the
male and female parents are independent, then this should just be equal to the
product:
\begin{equation}
(\#eq:denom-product)
P\bigl(I(A^1_\m) =  I(B^1_\m),~I(A^1_\f) =  I(B^1_\f)\bigr) = P\bigl(I(A^1_\m) =  I(B^1_\m) \bigr)P\bigl(I(A^1_\f) =  I(B^1_\f) \bigr)
\end{equation}
which should be easy to compute.

Hmmm...so, I had been thinking that it might be expedient to just go ahead and assume
that the probability of more than one lineage being shared at any particular time
depth in the pedigree was zero, because then those multiple sharing terms drop
away.  But, in fact, it looks like we might be able to make the less stringent
assumption that lineage sharing is independent between portions of the pedigree that
are not connected along the arrow paths: if we think of the pedigree as a dag with
arrows going down, then sharing between individuals that have to go "against an arrow"
in order to draw a line from one to the other would be considered independent.  Basically
that condition is that if you are already sharing one pair of ancestors, then the sharing of
another pair, neither of which are ancestors (or descendants) of the original pair,
would be considered independent.  All right.  Let's work with that.  


OK.  Let's restrict the problem a little bit to make it simpler to think about, and
then we can expand it later.  First, assume that the only relationships we will find
are of the $\HH{a}{b}$ variety, and _only with_ $a=b$.  So, we are not going to worry
about avunculars and things for the moment.  And assume that mating is totally at
random, so full sibs are independently obtained double half-sibs.  In this case, we
would trace upward from $A$ and $B$ accumulating probabilities. If we ever got to
a shared ancestor we would stop tracing up above that, because we know that the
ancestors above the shared one would always be the same.  So, if we are comparing
an ancestor in a later generation between $A$ and $B$, we are effectively saying
that the descendants of those ancestors were not shared at all between $A$ and $B$,
and that is the way it should be, because we are trying to compute the probability
of the first-hit ancestors.  But, the upshot of this rambling of mine is that any
time we are, say, looking at possible cohorts of the parents and asking if the
fathers of $A$ and $B$ or the mothers of $A$ and $B$ might be half-siblings (i.e.,
asking if they are shared grandparents of $A$ and $B$) we are going to be doing that
conditional on both $A$ and $B$ not having shared either the mother or the father.
So, the relevant conditional probability on the cohorts of the mother and father
will be that given in \@ref(eq:parent-cohorts-unshared), which can be calculated
quickly and easily from already computed quantities via the numerator, as given
in \@ref(eq:pcu-numer), and the denominator as given in \@ref(eq:pcu-denom) with the
joint probability term computed as in \@ref(eq:denom-product).

It is also interesting to note that if we are simply assuming that shared ancestors
in "non-vertical" parts of the pedigree are independent, then we can calculate the
probability of joint first-hit relationships in all the different pedigree subtrees.
This can be seen pretty easily by looking at the first pedigree figure.  If $A$ and
$B$ share an ancestor, then you can just ignore everything above each of those shared
first-hit ancestors, but then you have all the other non-ingored ancestors as possible
matches, too.  The denominator in the cohort probabilities is different, but
should be computable from cached quantities.   I feel like I have a pretty good
sense of how this would proceed in this restricted space where $a=b$.  (I haven't
written it out yet, but I will wait on that until we don't have that restriction).
In order to relieve ourselves of that restriction, I think it will be helpful to
talk about the probabilities of direct-descent relationships.  

Our notation extends nicely to this case.  We will use $I(A^0) = I(B^1_s)$ to denote
the situation in which $A$ is a sex-$s$ parent of $B$, and since these relationships
are not symmetrical we note that in the other direction it would be written as
$I(B^0) = I(A^1_s)$.  One defining feature of these sorts of direct relationships
is that both members of the pair have been directly sampled, and that figures into
the probability.  We will denote the sampling times as $S(A)$ and $S(B)$ respectively.
We write the probabilities down as:
$$
P\biggl(C(B^1_s),~I(A^0) = I(B^1_s)~\biggr|~ C(A^0), S(A),   \biggr)
$$
I don't want to write it all the way out at the moment, but basically the probability
that A is the sex-$s$ parent of $B$ boils down to the probability that $C(B^1_s)$ is equal
to the cohort of $A$ (that's an ERRO calculation) times the probability that $A$ is the
parent of $B$ from that cohort (that is a $1/N$ calculation) times the probability
that $A$ survived to the time of $B$'s birth, if $A$ was sampled before $B$'s birth.
That survival term is 1 if $A$ was sampled after $B$'s birth and 0 if $A$ was lethally
sampled before $B$'s birth, and can account for additional sampling mortality if
$A$ was sampled before $B$'s birth.  And, of course, if we have any covariates that
could affect the ERRO calculation (like length) we should use that.  That's a bit of a
hassle, but can be dealt with.


 

Now we are in a place to start walking through what the recursive algorithm
will be to compute these probabilities up the pedigree.
```{r}
sample_times <- tibble::tibble(
  indiv = c("A", "B-4"),
  cohort = c(56, 44),
  age = c(5, 3)
)

draw_pedigree_and_cohorts(
  sample_times = sample_times,
  cohortBarBlackText = TRUE,
  sexA = "M"
)
```

First, we have an initialization in which we calculate:
$$
P\biggl(I(A^1_s) = I(B^1_s)~\biggl|~ C(A) = c_A,~C(B)=c_B  \biggr)
$$
for $s\in\{\m,\f\}$ and for all $c_A$ and $c_B$ which are possible cohort pairs
for half-siblings going back $n-1$ generations.  In the process, we will, or course,
compute
$$
P\bigl(C(A^1_s) = c^s_A,~C(B^1_s) = c^s_B \mid
       I(A^1_s) \neq  I(B^1_s),~C(A) = c_A,~C(B) = c_B\bigl)
$$
for all $c_A$ and $c_B$ and both sexes $s$, and then also for the
$c^2_A$ and $c^2_B$ cohorts of the parents.  Once we have pre-computed those we
should be in a good position to quickly go back by one generation.  


We also need to compute similar quantities for going back one generation,
but only on either the $A$ or the $B$ side.  This is what the 



see which of $A$ or $B$ is older.  In the figure, $A$ is older so we evaluate
the probability that $A$ is the father of $B$.  


# Starting Over from Scratch

I spent a lot of time obsessing over this in the last few days, and doing some pencil
and paper work, and I think it is time to build this all up from the ground again
with different notation and a newfound perspective.  I am hoping that I can work
this out correctly this time.  In order to capture all the possibilities a little
bit better, visually---especially the chance for great-grandparent-great-grandchild
relationships---I will make a new figure that has early maturation times (1 year for
males and 2 for females):
```{r}
draw_pedigree_and_cohorts(
  cohortBarBlackText = TRUE,
  showCohorts = TRUE,
  sexA = "M", 
  Mf = 2,
  Mm = 1
)
```
The above shows a pedigree-cohort diagram extending back in time for $n=3$ generations
from sample $A$ and sample $B$ in a
population in which males mature at $M_\m=1$ and have a maximum reproductive age
of $A^\m_\mmax = 10$, while, for females, the corresponding values are
$M_\f=2$ and $A^\f_\mmax = 12$.

Each individual in the pedigree is referred to by a number from 1 to $2^{n+1}-1$, where
$n$ is the number of generations back from the samples the pedigrees extend. And,
more generally, the indexes of ancestors at depth $g>0$ generations before the sample run
from $2^g$ to $2^{g+1}-1$.
We note that the samples themselves may  be referred to by their index/number in the pedigree,
which is 1. So, individual 1 in $A$'s pedigree is sample $A$ itself.  We may refer to specific
individuals as, for example $Ax$ or $Bx$, where $x$ is the index of the individual in the
pedigree.  Hence, $A5$ would be the paternal grandmother of $A$, and $B1$ would be $B$
itself.  For $x>1$, even numbers are males and
odd numbers are females. Individual $x$ appears
$\modd{\log_2x}$ generations before the sample. Furthermore, $x$'s father has index
$2x$ and $x$'s mother has index $2x+1$, and thus, for $x>0$ the child of a male or
female $x$ has index $\modd{x/2}$.

We let the minimum and maximum feasible cohorts for an individual with index $x$ be denoted
$\cmin{x}$ and $\cmax{x}$, respectively, and we represent all the feasible cohorts for
$x$ as $[\cmin{x},\cmax{x}]$, the ordered set of integers from $\cmin{x}$ to $\cmax{x}$, inclusive.
We take the cohorts of the samples themselves
to be known with certainty (age uncertainty is added after the multigenerational kinship
calculation), such that, for $A1$ we have $\cmin{1}=\cmax{1}=c_A$ and for $B1$,
$\cmin{1}=\cmax{1}=c_B$. When we wish to refer to a range of feasible cohorts for
individual $x$ within a specific pedigree, like $A$'s, we will use the $Ax$ notation,
for example, $[\cmin{Ax},\cmax{Ax}]$. The feasible cohorts for an individual with $x>1$ can 
be obtained from the feasible cohorts of their child with index $k=\modd{x/2}$ by:
\begin{equation}
(\#eq:cminmax)
[\cmin{x},\cmax{x}] =
\begin{cases}
[\cmin{k}-M_\m,\cmax{k}-A^\m_\mmax]~,~~~\mbox{if}~x~\mbox{is even} \\
[\cmin{k}-M_\f,\cmax{k}-A^\f_\mmax]~,~~~\mbox{if}~x~\mbox{is odd}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
The above gives the feasible cohorts to which an ancestor may belong.  We also
want to speak of the probability that an individual is in a certain cohort.  We
define this as a conditional probability that $x$ is of cohort $c$ given that
its child $k$ was born in cohort $c^*$.  For $x>1$ these probabilities are
proportional to the expected relative reproductive output (ERRO) of the individuals of cohort
$c$ in the year $c^*$.
\begin{equation}
(\#eq:pxk)
p^x_k(c,c^*) \propto
\begin{cases}
E_{\m,c^*,c^*-c}~,~~~\mbox{if}~x~\mbox{is even and~} c^*-A^\m_\mmax < c < c^*-M_\m \\
E_{\f,c^*,c^*-c}~,~~~\mbox{if}~x~\mbox{is odd and~} c^*-A^\f_\mmax < c < c^*-M_\f \\
0~,~~~\mbox{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
with equality obtained by normalizing so that $p^x_k(c,c^*)$ sums to 1 over $c$. 
$E_{s,t,a}$ is the ERRO of all the sex-$s$ and age-$a$ individuals
alive at time $t$, a familiar term in CKMR.

Samples $A$ and $B$ are related to one another if there exist an individual with
index $x$ in $A$'s pedigree that is the same individual as an individual with
index $y$ in $B$'s pedigree. In order for $x$ and $y$ to be same individual, it
must be the case that $x$ and $y$ are from the same cohort and that $x$ and $y$ are
the same sex (species that do not change sex).  We denote by $S^x_y(c)$ the event that $x$ in
$A$'s pedigree and $y$ in $B$'s are the same individual born in cohort $c$. The figure
above is instructive because it shows visually the individuals in $A$'s pedigree
that could come from the same cohort and be of the same sex as individuals in $B$'s
pedigree.  For example, $A1$, born in 56 could be any one of the male's in $B$'s
pedigree whose range of feasible cohorts includes 56; in order from left to write
those are 8, 4, 2, 10, 12 and 6.  

In order to maintain simplicity and computational efficiency, we will assume that
$A$ and $B$ share either a single most recent ancestor or two most recent ancestors
that occur in no more than a single mating. We have
to say "most recent" here, because the ancestors of any shared ancestor will also
be shared.  Thus, loosely following the 
notation of @skare2009identification, $A$ and $B$ can
share a single relationship characterized either as $\HH{a}{b}$, where $A$ and
$B$ share a single most-recent ancestor that is $a$ generations from $A$ and $b$ generations
from $B$; or characterized as $\FF{a}{b}$, where $A$ and $B$ share two most-recent ancestors
at a depth of $a$ and $b$ generations from $A$ and $B$, and those two ancestors
mated to produce $A$ and $B$ or individuals that are ancestors to $A$ and $B$.
For example, $\HH{1}{1}$ is a half-sibling relationship, $\FF{1}{1}$ is a full-sibling
relationship, $\HH{1}{2}$ is a half avuncular relationship, $\FF{3}{3}$ is a full
second cousin relationship, and so on.  For the
$H$-type relationships, we allow either or both of $a$ and $b$ to be zero.  Hence,
$\HH{0}{0}$ indicates that $A$ and $B$ are the same individual (or are clones),
$\HH{0}{b}$ means that $A$ is a direct ancestor, $b$ generations ago, of $B$, and
$\HH{a}{0}$ means that $B$ is a direct ancestor of $A$, $a$ generations back from $A$.
Another way of stating this is that
the relationships we allow between $A$ and $B$ are characterized by only a single
one of the four possible mutually exclusive cases:

* $A$ and $B$ are from the same cohort and are the same individual.
* The younger of $A$ or $B$ is a direct descendant of the older of $A$ or $B$.
* A single ancestor of $A$ and a single ancestor of $B$ are half-siblings.
* A single ancestor of $A$ and a single ancestor of $B$ are full-siblings.

Because the occurrence of any shared ancestor occurs with probability of
order $O(1/N)$, this assumption is equivalent to ignoring events with probability
on the order of $O(1/N^2)$, which is already common in CKMR studies of
large marine populations.
